nodes.name: Flame-assisted RuO2 deposition
nodes.procedure: 20 mg of KB was weighed and placed onto a 2×10 cm² glass slide. The KB was then uniformly spread and pressed flat with a spatula to a thickness not exceeding 5 mm. Next, a RuCl3 solution in ethanol at a concentration of 10 mg ml⁻¹ was prepared, and 400 μl of this solution was drawn into a pipette. Under open-air conditions, the solution was added dropwise from a height of approximately 5 mm above the KB layer, with each drop controlled to a volume of 15-20 μl to minimize powder dispersal. The slide was then left undisturbed until the solution was fully absorbed by the KB. Subsequently, the wetted material was ignited in air, where ethanol combustion generated a transient inner flame (~228°C) that yielded uniformly dispersed RuO2 nanoclusters (~1.03 nm) on KB. Upon complete extinction of the flame, the resulting powder was collected, yielding the KB@Ru composite.

nodes.name: Phosphorization at 300°C
nodes.procedure: An amount of 0.3 g of NaH2PO2 was weighed into a porcelain boat and placed in front of the porcelain boat containing KB@Ru near the gas inlet of a tube furnace. The samples were then heated at a rate of 5°C min⁻¹ to 300°C and maintained at these temperatures for 2 h under nitrogen atmosphere. The final products obtained were designated as KB@RuP-300.

nodes.name: Colloidal milling scalable synthesis
nodes.procedure: A total of 10 g of KB and 200 ml of RuCl3 ethanolic solution (6 mg ml⁻¹ in ethanol) were incrementally added into a colloid mill. The rotation speed of the colloid mill was set to 4,500 rpm, and after milling for 5 min, a uniform slurry was obtained. This slurry was evenly applied as a thin layer onto an insulated glass plate, followed by an ignition treatment. The powder resulting from the ignition was collected and subjected to the same phosphorization process at 800°C in a tube furnace as previously described, ultimately yielding KB@RuP-800-B.

nodes.characterization_summary: SEM analysis revealed that all phosphatized samples retain the uniform KB spheres without obvious Ru particle aggregations.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis revealed that all phosphatized samples retain the uniform KB spheres without obvious Ru particle aggregations (Fig. 1b,f,j).

nodes.characterization_summary: High-resolution TEM images reveal that the phosphating process transforms KB@Ru from RuO2 clusters into 3.1-9.4 nm particles containing Ru–O and Ru–P components with tunable core–shell architecture.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Additionally, high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images reveal that the phosphating process transforms KB@Ru from RuO2 clusters into 3.1-9.4 nm particles containing two distinct components: Ru–O and Ru–P.

nodes.characterization_summary: HAADF-STEM shows distinct core–shell structures for KB@RuP-800 and KB@RuP-550 with shell thickness decreasing from ~3 nm to <1 nm as phosphating temperature increases to 800°C.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) was employed to investigate the atomic structures of the RuP particles.

nodes.characterization_summary: Selected-area STEM with FFT reveals shell lattice spacing corresponds to (200) plane of RuP2 and core to (111) plane of RuO2 for KB@RuP-800 and KB@RuP-550.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Furthermore, selected-area STEM combined with fast Fourier transform (FFT) images reveals that the lattice spacing of the shell ... aligns with the (111) plane of RuO2 (Fig. 1i,m).

nodes.characterization_summary: EDX mapping and elemental line scans confirm P-enriched shell that becomes thinner with increasing phosphating temperature.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Moreover, energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) mapping and elemental line scans further confirm a P-enriched shell that becomes thinner with increasing phosphating temperature (Supplementary Figs. 7–11).

nodes.characterization_summary: XRD patterns show RuP2 ((110), (020), (101)) and RuO2 ((111), (112)) phases in KB@RuP-800 and KB@RuP-550; KB@RuP-300 and KB@Ru show only carbon patterns.
nodes.evidence_snippet: X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns pinpoint the existence of RuP2 ... and RuO2 ... in KB@RuP-800 and KB@RuP-550 (Fig. 2a).

nodes.characterization_summary: P 2p XPS after Ar sputtering confirms lowest Ru–P content in KB@RuP-800, verifying thinner RuP2 shell.
nodes.evidence_snippet: To minimize surface-oxide interference, P 2p spectra collected after Ar sputtering further confirm the lowest Ru–P content in KB@RuP-800 (ref. 17; Fig. 2c).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru K-edge XANES shows valence state between RuO2 and RuP2, increasing with phosphating temperature; phosphorus reduces Ru valence compared to RuO2.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 2d, the Ru K-edge energy of KB@RuP-800 and the other phosphated samples is located between those of RuO2 and RuP2, indicating that the valence state of Ru lies between 0 and +4.

nodes.characterization_summary: EXAFS shows Ru–O peaks at ~1.5 Å and Ru–P at 1.8 Å; Ru–P coordination decreases and Ru–O increases with phosphating temperature, confirming RuP2 shell thinning.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 2f, KB@RuP-800, KB@RuP-550, KB@RuP-300 and KB@Ru all display characteristic Ru–O coordination peaks at approximately 1.5 Å ... Additionally, pronounced Ru–P coordination peaks are observed at 1.8 Å.

nodes.characterization_summary: In situ XRD shows blueshift in RuO2 (111) plane of KB@RuP-800 with increasing overpotential, suggesting H intercalation into RuO2 lattice.
nodes.evidence_snippet: For KB@RuP-800, a noticeable blueshift in the RuO2 (111) crystal plane was observed with increasing overpotential (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 39).

nodes.characterization_summary: In situ Raman shows steeper Stark tuning rates for KB@RuP-800 (4-HB-H2O: -0.38 cm/mV, 2-HB-H2O: -0.16, Free-HB-H2O: 0.26) than KB@RuP-550, indicating enhanced interfacial water reorganization.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Stark tuning on KB@RuP-800 is steeper than on KB@RuP-550 for the following water environments: 4-HB-H2O (−0.38 versus −0.08 cm mV−1), 2-HB-H2O (−0.16 versus −0.05) and Free-HB-H2O (0.26 versus 0.12).

nodes.characterization_summary: AFM images show rough electrode surface of KB@RuP-800 promotes gas transport and rapid bubble detachment at high current densities.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Based on the analysis of bubble overflow (Fig. 3g) and surface roughness (atomic force microscopy (AFM) images; Fig. 3g).

nodes.characterization_summary: ICP analysis of electrolytes after cycling detects [Ru] of 1.22 mg L⁻¹ and 1.19 mg L⁻¹ for KB@Ru and KB@RuP-300 vs 0.008 and 0.005 mg L⁻¹ for KB@RuP-550 and KB@RuP-800.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Analysis of the electrolytes after cycling, using ICP, detected a high [Ru] of 1.22 and 1.19 mg l⁻¹ for KB@Ru and KB@RuP-300, versus 0.008 and 0.005 mg l⁻¹ for KB@RuP-550 and KB@RuP-800.
